The Western trumpeter sillago (Sillago burrus) is a demersal marine fish found in coastal and estuarine waters of northern Australia and southern Papua New Guinea, where it supports modest commercial and recreational fisheries. Like many sillaginids, this species exhibits a life history that is tightly coupled to seasonal thermal regimes. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], the incubation period from fertilisation through yolk-sac resorption is remarkably brief, with the yolk-dependent prolarvae emerging from the chorion and commencing the transition to exogenous feeding in approximately 3 days [ab = approximately 3 days]. At the moment of hatching, the newly emerged yolk-sac larvae possess a minute body mass of approximately 0.00015 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00015 grams]. This initial wet weight at birth, typical of marine teleosts producing small, pelagic eggs, reflects the energetic constraints of a yolk volume that sustains the larva only until mouth opening, at which point it must capture its first prey.

Following the completion of larval metamorphosis and the transition to a benthic juvenile existence, immature individuals of Sillago burrus grow rapidly on shallow sand flats and seagrass beds. Growth in length, which forms the basis for age estimation in this species, is asymptotic: the largest individuals recorded in field surveys attain a maximum fork length of 36 centimeters [Li = 36 centimeters]. This ultimate size, derived from length-frequency analysis of commercial catches, is comparable to that reported for other large sillaginids and is reached after several years of sustained somatic expansion. However, reproductive activity commences well before this terminal size is approached. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from wild-caught specimens indicates that the onset of spermatogenesis and vitellogenesis occurs when fish reach a body length of approximately 13.4 centimeters fork length [Lp = approximately 13.4 centimeters fork length], a threshold that is consistently observed across multiple sampling locations and seasons.

The fecundity of breeding females is substantial, reflecting a life-history strategy focused on high early reproductive output. A single gravid female can contain approximately 150,000 vitellogenic oocytes that are released during a single spawning event, yielding a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 410,958 oocytes per month [Ri = approximately 410,958 oocytes per month] At the stable thermal regime of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], which characterises the species' spawning season in tropical Australian waters, the period between successive spawning events is relatively short, with field studies indicating that individual females undergo approximately 1.5 spawning events per month throughout the extended reproductive season. This combination of high batch fecundity and frequent spawning, when integrated across the entire breeding window, yields a substantial annual reproductive investment that is characteristic of many tropical demersal spawners. The resulting reproductive rate per individual is typical of a highly fecund, iteroparous marine fish.

With respect to somatic growth and ultimate body dimensions, the relationship between fork length and wet weight in Sillago burrus follows a conventional allometric power function. Applying this length-weight relationship to the maximum recorded length of 36 centimeters [Li = 36 centimeters] yields a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 510.2 grams [Wwi = 510.2 grams], representing the heaviest body mass attainable by a fully grown adult. This asymptotic mass is seldom observed in exploited populations, where size-selective fishing pressure tends to truncate the age structure, but it provides a useful benchmark for assessing the species' growth potential under pristine conditions. Body condition indices calculated from field-caught individuals typically approach this value only in the largest and oldest animals, which are predominantly females in the post-pubertal size classes. The allometric exponent for this species aligns closely with values reported for other members of the family Sillaginidae, reinforcing the utility of this morphometric relationship.

The natural lifespan of Western trumpeter sillago in the wild, based on otolith-based age validation studies and mark-recapture data from unfished populations, extends to a maximum of approximately 2,920 days [am = approximately 2,920 days] when individuals experience the optimal thermal regime of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C] throughout their lives. This longevity corresponds to roughly eight years, a duration that places this species among the longer-lived members of the genus Sillago, though still modest compared to some temperate demersal fishes. The oldest individuals collected in fishery-independent surveys have been aged at well over five years, confirming that the maximum lifespan exceeds earlier estimates based solely on length-frequency distributions. This extended lifespan, coupled with the high annual fecundity described previously, suggests that the species possesses a considerable capacity for population resilience, provided that spawning stock biomass is maintained above critical thresholds by appropriate fisheries management measures.
